title: Krishna Defies the Conspirators
story:
Krishna had come to Hastinapura as the messenger of the five Pandavas, to ask their cousins the Kauravas for peace; and Duryodhana, the eldest of the cousins, had answered by plotting to seize him. Now the plot lay open. Satyaki's warning had carried it into the crowded hall of the Kurus, and every eye in the assembly turned to the man who had been its target. The four conspirators were not there to hear the secret spoken — they had left the court to shape their plan — but Krishna sat as though he had heard nothing worth troubling over, without moving a muscle of his face. The hall fell so quiet that the breathing of the mailed men at the door could be heard.

Krishna cast his eyes on Dhritarashtra and spoke, in the hearing of them all.

"King," he said, "if these men wish to punish me with force, let them punish me. As for my punishing them — I can master all of them together, however wild with rage they are. But I will not commit an act that is sinful and shameful."

He paused, and the court felt the whole meaning of his words settle over it: he had not asked for protection, had not called on the troops, had not even risen from his seat. Threats had been hurled across that hall for months, but no one had ever answered one like this — with the calm of a man describing the weather while holding the outcome in his hand.

"Your sons covet the possessions of the Pandavas," he went on, "and by coveting them they will lose their own. If they truly desire this deed, then Yudhishthira's aim will be accomplished easily enough — for this very day I could seize these men with all who follow them and hand them over to the sons of Pritha, their mother Kunti. What is hard for me? But I will not, in your presence, great king, do a deed that springs only from anger and a wicked mind. Let it be as Duryodhana wishes. I give all your sons permission to try."

A sound went through the hall that was half wonder and half fear. The court had grown used to Krishna the negotiator — a voice asking for an agreement. The man who sat before them now could end the quarrel between the two houses with a single motion, and chose instead to hold himself back. He was not refusing the plot because he feared it. He was refusing to meet it on its own ground. And in that refusal the truth became clear to everyone present: the conspiracy had not failed because it had been discovered. It had failed because it was impossible — and had been impossible from the moment it was conceived.

Dhritarashtra sat blind and silent, his face turned toward the voice. Then the old king found his answer. "Vidura," he said, "bring Duryodhana here at once — the boy so hungry for sovereignty — with his friends, his counsellors, his brothers, his followers. I will see whether, with one more effort, I can set him on the right path."

So Vidura went out again and brought back the unwilling Duryodhana, ringed by Karna and Dussasana and the kings who followed him. The prince came in with his face set, and the crowd pressing after him filled the aisles, so that the hushed court grew restless once more — men shifting, weapons clinking, every face turned toward father and son.

The defiance hung in the air of the assembly like a drawn blade. Krishna had given his permission — the calmest, most terrible permission ever spoken in that hall. And Dhritarashtra, grasping at his son, was making one last attempt to keep the peace from breaking. Whether it would hold, no one in that hall could say.
reflection: The striking thing about Krishna's answer is what it refuses to do: he does not rage at the plot, does not threaten the plotters, does not even protect himself. He grants them permission to try, and names his own restraint — not his power — as the only boundary he will not cross. Power held in check, he suggests, is the greater demonstration.
next_story_tease: Duryodhana's answer to that permission would draw from Krishna a sight no one in the court had ever seen.
hero_scene: Krishna, calm and unmoved in the midst of the Kuru assembly, looks directly at blind Dhritarashtra and gives his sons permission to try to seize him, while the court holds its breath.
